The Complainants allege the violation of the provisions of Articles 4, 5, 6, and 23(1) of the African Charter.

The Complainants request the African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights (the Commission) to declare that Côte d'Ivoire has violated the provisions of the aforementioned Articles of the African Charter. They further request the Commission to order the Respondent State to: - Restore the rule of law as soon as possible; - Promptly conduct investigations into the established cases of violations of the rights guaranteed by the African Charter; - Try those guilty of abuses and mass violations of human rights; - Grant reparation to the victims while recognising their status; - Guarantee the security of human rights defenders and their activities; - Restore and guarantee peace throughout the national territory.
With particular regard to the Duékoué massacres, the Complainants request the Commission to refer the matter to the African Court on Human and Peoples' Rights.

The Complaint reached the Secretariat on 3 May 2011. At its 49 Ordinary Session, held from 28 April to 12 May 2011 in Banjul, The Gambia, the Commission considered the Complaint and decided to be seized of it. The Parties were informed of this decision and the Secretariat requested the Complainants to submit their observations on Admissibility.
On 29 October 2011, the Complainants transmitted their observations on Admissibility. The Secretariat transmitted a copy to the Respondent State and requested its defence brief.

At its 51 Ordinary Session held from 18 April to 02 May 2012, in Banjul, The Gambia, the Commission considered the Communication and decided to adjourn for lack of the Respondent State's brief. The Parties were informed of this decision and a reminder was sent to the Respondent State. At its 52 Ordinary Session held from 09 to 22 October 2012 in Yamoussoukro, Côte d'Ivoire, the Commission again deferred the matter for the same reasons. The related correspondence was transmitted to the Parties.

On 17 October 2012, the Respondent State transmitted its defence brief. The Secretariat acknowledged receipt of it and transmitted it to the Complainants for their reply. On 13 December 2012, the Complainants transmitted their response to the Secretariat, which forwarded a copy to the Respondent State.

At its 53 Ordinary Session held from 09 to 23 April 2013, in Banjul, The Gambia, the Commission considered the Communication and decided to defer it to allow for the preparation of a decision on Admissibility. The Parties were informed of the Commission's decision. Having considered the Communication at its successive sessions, the Commission decided to defer its decision owing to time constraints. The Secretariat transmitted the usual correspondence to the Parties.

At its 16 Extraordinary Session held from 20 to 29 July 2014 in Kigali, Rwanda, the Commission considered a draft decision on Admissibility and decided to adjourn the file to its next session for the finalisation of its decision.

While alleging that the Communication complies with all the admissibility requirements set out in Article 56 of the African Charter, the Complainants dwell particularly on those prescribed in Articles 56(4), 56(5) and 56(7).

To prove compliance with the provisions of Article 56(4), the Complainants indicate that the alleged facts are recorded in reports, notably the Report of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights on the situation in Côte d'Ivoire and the Report of the United Nations International Independent Commission of Inquiry that investigated the human rights violations committed following the 2010 presidential election. The Complainants also refer to numerous testimonies of Ivorians who were present in Côte d'Ivoire during the events reported in the Complaint.

Referring to the Commission's decision in the case of Jawara v. The Gambia, the Complainants maintain that the crucial question is not whether the information contained in the Communication comes from the media but rather whether the said information is accurate and whether the Complainant has verified it.

As regards the requirement of exhaustion of local remedies laid down in Article 56(5), the Complainants allege that the said remedies must be considered as having been exhausted. In support of this allegation, they mainly argue that the authorities of the Respondent State "were not competent to hear this case, since they could not be both judge and party". The Complainants observe in this regard that the national courts have no jurisdiction over crimes against humanity and mass violations of human rights, acts falling within the jurisdiction of the International Criminal Court. They cite in particular the provisions of the Constitution of Côte d'Ivoire relating to the indictment of the President of the Republic before the High Court of Justice, a court bound by the definition of crimes resulting from the criminal laws in force at the time of the events. According to the Complainants, as national law provides for no procedure concerning mass violations of human rights, the domestic courts cannot have jurisdiction to hear the facts alleged in the Communication.

In the alternative, the Complainants argue, referring to the Commission's jurisprudence, that given the large number of victims and the scale and diversity of the violations, it "was difficult for the national courts to offer effective remedies". Insisting that they invoke the rights of peoples, the Complainants further allege that only the Commission has jurisdiction to hear the violation thereof, the jurisdiction of the national courts relating rather to individual rights. They conclude that the Commission should have primacy to hear the alleged violations, on the basis in particular of actio popularis.

Without contesting the serious and massive nature of the violations alleged by the Complainants, the Respondent State considers it excessive to maintain that such violations are attributable to the State on the sole ground that it failed in its obligation to protect the rights concerned. According to the Respondent State, the Communication refers to a period during which Côte d'Ivoire was going through a crisis that weakened its institutions to the point where it was difficult for it to honour its international commitments, including those of protecting the rights guaranteed under the African Charter.

On the basis of this preliminary point, the Respondent State mainly alleges that the Communication is unfounded. In support of the ground of lack of foundation, Côte d'Ivoire maintains that its obligations under the Charter do not imply that violations cannot be perpetrated on its territory, but rather require it to take all necessary measures so that such violations do not go unpunished.

In this regard, the Respondent State maintains that the obligation thus set out has been duly fulfilled since it has undertaken or is in the process of undertaking all the necessary measures so that those responsible for the violations perpetrated during the electoral and post-electoral period are tried. To prove this, Côte d'Ivoire reports that, upon the return to normality, President Alassane Ouattara committed himself, on 1 June 2011, to restoring the authority of the State and combating the impunity of the perpetrators of the violations to which the Communication refers. The Respondent State thus indicates that, after recognising the jurisdiction of the International Criminal Court, the Government set up, by Decree No. 2011-176 of 20 July 2011, the National Commission of Inquiry into violations of Human Rights and International Humanitarian Law (the Commission of Inquiry) that occurred after the 2010 presidential election. On the basis of the Report submitted by the Commission of Inquiry on 08 August 2012, the President of the Republic immediately instructed the Minister of Justice to take judicial action on the conclusions of the said Report.

In conclusion, the Respondent State requests the Commission to find that it has taken and is taking the appropriate measures to prosecute before the competent national courts the perpetrators of human rights violations whose responsibility has been established. It therefore requests that the Communication be declared inadmissible for non-exhaustion of local remedies and lack of foundation.

In response to the Respondent State's observations, the Complainants take note of the investigative measures undertaken by the Government of Côte d'Ivoire with a view to prosecuting the perpetrators of the alleged violations. However, the Complainants deplore the absence of a timetable for the investigation of the related cases.

Furthermore, the Complainants admit the existence of local remedies but maintain that the Respondent State is required to prove the effectiveness and sufficiency of the said remedies. Referring to their initial submissions, they insist on the incompetence of the domestic courts to hear serious and massive human rights violations. They note in this regard the Respondent State's failure to specify the legal provisions on the basis of which the indicated prosecutions were undertaken.

This Communication was submitted in accordance with Article 55 of the African Charter, which gives the Commission jurisdiction to receive and consider "communications other than those of States parties". To be declared admissible, such communications must meet the requirements laid down in Article 56 of the African Charter.

Upon examination of the arguments they invoke, it appears to the Commission that the Parties agree that the Communication complies with all the admissibility requirements set out in Article 56 of the African Charter, with the exception of the one prescribing the exhaustion of local remedies. As regards the other admissibility requirements, the Commission finds for itself that the Communication complies with them. Consequently, the examination of admissibility will relate exclusively to the requirement of exhaustion of local remedies laid down in Article 56(5) of the African Charter.

Under the terms of the said Article, a Communication must necessarily, in order to be declared admissible, be submitted after exhaustion of local remedies, if any, unless it is obvious that this procedure is unduly prolonged. Furthermore, the Commission consistently holds that, where they exist, the remedies whose exhaustion is required must be available, effective and sufficient in order to comply with the provisions of Article 56(5) of the African Charter.

Apart from these exceptions, the Commission has also concluded, for example in the cases of Malawi African Association and Others v. Mauritania and Sudan Human Rights Organisation and Another v. Sudan concerning serious and massive violations of human rights, that the requirement of exhaustion of local remedies cannot apply where it is neither practicable, that is, possible or feasible, nor desirable for the Complainant to pursue the said remedies. However, in order to grasp the merits of this exception, one must go back to the leading decision in Malawi African Association, by which the Commission introduced it in the following terms: The Commission does not believe that the requirement of exhaustion of local remedies applies literally in cases where it is impractical or undesirable for the complainants or the victims to seize the domestic courts in the case of each violation. This is the case where there are a large number of victims. Due to the seriousness of the human rights situation in Mauritania as well as the great number of people involved, such remedies are as a matter of fact unavailable.

The Commission notes that it emerges from this precedent that it is the impracticable or impossible nature of the exhaustion of local remedies that may contribute to characterising a situation of massive human rights violations as a ground for derogation from the requirement laid down in Article 56(5) of the African Charter. It goes without saying that where the exhaustion of local remedies is possible or feasible, the serious or massive nature of the violations cannot, on its own, constitute a ground for exemption from seizing the competent and available domestic courts.

This position is well confirmed by the consistent international human rights jurisprudence on the rationale for the exception to the exhaustion of local remedies, including in cases of serious and massive violations. Thus in Arhuacos v. Colombia, the United Nations Human Rights Committee exempted the Complainant from exhausting local remedies in a case of serious violation - right to life and torture - because the available remedies had been found inadequate and ineffective owing to their disciplinary and administrative nature.

In a similar approach, and like the Committee, the European Court of Human Rights has consistently held, inter alia in Akdivar and Others v. Turkey, that in cases of serious and massive human rights violations, there is a presumption of ineffectiveness of local remedies. However, the Court bases this presumption on the fact that the rule of law is no longer respected domestically when rights are systematically violated. The Court itself recognises that it is only a presumption which, not being irrebuttable, must be proved by the Complainant. By way of illustration of situations in which the exception to the exhaustion of local remedies applies, the Court moreover cites its case law in Ireland v. the United Kingdom. In that precedent, the Court adopts the position that the exception applies where the violation at issue results from "a repetitive administrative practice, tolerated by the Respondent State and of such a nature as to make remedies futile or ineffective".

The Commission notes that the practicability of local remedies may be both theoretical and practical. In theory, the exhaustion of remedies is possible only where the said remedies exist legally, that is, where they are provided for by law or any other mechanisms put in place in the domestic system of the Respondent State. In practice, the remedies must be capable, notably from a material, technical or logistical point of view, of examining the cases of alleged violations and of remedying them. In the present Communication, it is for the Commission to verify whether, as the Complainants maintain, it was not or has not been either possible or desirable to pursue local remedies in theory and in practice.

As regards the possibility of pursuing remedies in theory, the Complainants allege that neither the Constitution nor any other national law contains provisions giving the domestic courts jurisdiction to hear cases of massive human rights violations. They consider that only the Commission is competent to hear the present dispute. In plain terms, by such an argument, the Complainants seek to have it concluded that the mere fact that Ivorian domestic law does not specifically provide for the prosecution of cases of massive violations entails a lack of jurisdiction of the domestic courts regarding such violations.

On the question of jurisdiction, the Commission is rather of the view that, according to the well-known principle of international law of "subsidiarity" or "complementarity", domestic courts or mechanisms have primacy of jurisdiction over the international mechanisms recognised by the Respondent State. Thus, whatever the gravity of the violations perpetrated and whether they are violations of human rights or of international criminal law, the domestic courts of the Respondent State must first have the opportunity to remedy the situation. This sacrosanct rule of international litigation is enshrined in the sphere of criminal law by the principle that an international court may prosecute only where the State concerned is unwilling or unable to do so. By way of illustration, the provisions of Article 17 of the Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court stipulate that "the Court shall determine that a case is inadmissible where the case is being investigated or prosecuted by a State which has jurisdiction over it, unless the State is unwilling or unable genuinely to carry out the investigation or prosecution".

The same rule is reflected in the principle aut dedere aut iudicare adopted in a number of international treaties and notably as regards universal jurisdiction to prosecute acts of torture under the United Nations Convention against Torture and Other Cruel, Inhuman or Degrading Treatment or Punishment. Indeed, the provisions of Article 7(1) of the said Convention stipulate that "The State Party in the territory under whose jurisdiction a person alleged to have committed any such offence is found shall in the cases contemplated in article 4, if it does not extradite him, submit the case to its competent authorities for the purpose of prosecution". In this regard, the Commission notes that, as confirmed by the International Court of Justice in the case of Belgium v. Senegal, the rule of "prosecute or extradite" clearly means that prosecution by an international court or a third State is available as an alternative option only in the event that the State concerned has been unable to prosecute.

The Commission observes that international human rights law does not depart from the principle of subsidiarity or complementarity. Respect for subsidiarity is precisely the rationale of the rule of exhaustion of local remedies adopted by the United Nations Treaty Bodies as well as by the organs of the European and Inter-American human rights systems. In the African system, the Commission has laid down the underpinnings of the rule by deciding, for example, in World Organisation Against Torture and Others v. Rwanda, that "the requirement of exhaustion of local remedies is founded, among other things, on the principle that the Government concerned must be notified of a human rights violation in order to have the opportunity to remedy such violation before being called before an international body". Better still, the Commission extended the scope of the rationale of the rule of exhaustion of local remedies by holding in Amnesty International and Others v. Sudan that this rule "also prevents the Commission from becoming a tribunal of first instance, a function which it cannot assume either legally or in practice".

On these legal foundations and in the light of these precedents, the Commission is of the view that the domestic courts of the Respondent State have primary jurisdiction to hear violations of the rights guaranteed by the African Charter, whether individual or massive violations, unless a Complainant proves the impossibility of pursuing local remedies, in law or in fact. In the present Communication, the Complainants do not provide proof, by any of the arguments they invoke, that Ivorian legislation prohibits legal action on the sole basis of the serious or massive nature of the alleged violation. The provisions of Article 112 of the Ivorian Constitution cited by the Complainants are inapplicable in this case, in that they relate not to the jurisdiction of the national courts to hear cases of massive violations but rather to the procedure for prosecuting the President of the Republic and other members of the Government before the High Court of Justice for offences clearly defined both by the Constitution and by national criminal law.

Furthermore, the violations alleged by the Complainants include offences such as rape, murder and other acts provided for and punished by the domestic legislation of the Respondent State. These are therefore offences over which the domestic courts have full jurisdiction. The Commission observes in this regard that the terminology of "serious and massive violations" is not emblematic of international law or domestic law but must simply be understood as a characterisation of the character and nature of certain offences that require a particular legal and judicial response. In any event, national courts may well have jurisdiction to hear violations of a serious nature and massive scale provided that the related offences are provided for and punished by the criminal legislation of the State concerned. The Complainants have been unable to prove that this is not the case here. As a consequence of the foregoing, the Commission cannot accept the Complainants' argument that the domestic courts lack jurisdiction for the sole reason that the violations are massive.

With regard to the possibility of pursuing local remedies in practice, the Commission notes that the arguments developed by the Respondent State tend to prove that the said remedies exist. The State reports in this regard a series of measures undertaken by the new Government immediately after the end of the crisis during which the alleged violations were perpetrated. Cited among others are, on the one hand, the recognition on 1 June 2011 of the jurisdiction of the International Criminal Court and, on the other, the establishment, by a decree of 20 July 2011, of a National Commission of Inquiry tasked with shedding light on the human rights violations, including those alleged by the Complainants. The Respondent State further reports that upon receipt on 8 August 2012 of the Report of the said Commission of Inquiry, the President of the Republic immediately instructed the Minister of Justice to take judicial action on its conclusions.

While duly taking note of these actions undertaken by the Government of the Respondent State with a view to remedying the violations alleged by the Complainants, the Commission considers that they are of no relevance in the examination of the question to be resolved in this case. Indeed, that question is not whether the remedies existed at the date of filing of the submissions or whether they exist at the date of the present examination, but rather whether they existed prior to the seizure of the Commission. On this point, the Commission refers to its jurisprudence reported supra to note that the exhaustion of local remedies is obviously a precondition to the submission of the Complaint that initiates a Communication. Even though, in this case, neither of the Parties expressly answers the question thus determined, the Commission considers that it should be settled in order to conclude on Admissibility. Considering that the submissions filed by the Parties reveal the existence of concordant information capable of clarifying the question raised, it is appropriate to refer to them for that purpose.

In this regard, the Commission notes that, in this case, a series of key dates provides the evidentiary anchor for determining the existence of local remedies. At the end of the second round of the presidential election held on 28 November 2010, the results proclaimed on 2 December 2010 declared Mr Alassane Ouattara the winner. However, he was unable to take office because of the contestation of the results by the incumbent President, Mr Laurent Gbagbo.

The military armed conflict that followed these events, the civil hostilities and the ensuing violence lasted nearly five months until the arrest of President Laurent Gbagbo on 11 April 2011. Officially, this arrest ended the armed conflict and marked the beginning of a return to normality of the State in Côte d'Ivoire. The present Communication was submitted on 3 May 2011, that is, about a month after the end of hostilities and the establishment of the authority of the elected President.

From this dated breakdown of the events that marked the time frame of the violations, it appears to the Commission that certain major conclusions are inescapable regarding the existence of local remedies and the possibility of their exhaustion. First, the Complainants had time to witness the violations unfold, which extended over nearly five months. Second, the serious and massive nature of the violations was known to the Complainants, as was the alleged incompetence of the domestic courts. Finally, at the date of submission of the Complaint, the main cause of the instability and fragility of the State no longer existed.

The Commission notes that, despite their knowledge of the incompetence of the domestic courts owing to the serious and massive violations, the Complainants nevertheless did not seize the Commission during the five months that the post-electoral crisis lasted, although they were fully free to do so. This failure to act undermines the argument seeking an exception to the rule of exhaustion of local remedies on the ground of the non-existence of the said remedies.

While reaffirming that the rule of exhaustion of local remedies is neither absolute nor automatic, the Commission considers that, in examining compliance with this requirement, it is essential to pay particular attention to the specific circumstances of each case. On this point, the Commission agrees with the European Court of Human Rights when it concludes in the Akdivar case that "... the Court must take realistic account not only of the existence of formal remedies in the legal system of the Contracting Party concerned but also of the general legal and political context in which they operate as well as the personal circumstances of the applicants". Notably, in the Akdivar case, the Court had based its opinion mainly on the fact that the internal civil conflict that caused the alleged violations was still ongoing at the date of seizure. It is undeniable that, in such circumstances, the presumption of the non-existence or at least of the ineffectiveness of local remedies must be presumed. The circumstances are quite different in the present Communication.

In this case, the presumption of the non-existence of remedies cannot operate since the Complaint was submitted nearly a month after the conflict had come to an end. Failing an attempt to exhaust the remedies, it was incumbent on the Complainants to prove that the situation of conflict still existed at the date of the Complaint and that there was no reason to envisage the availability of local remedies. The Complainants' tendency seems rather to consist in requiring the Respondent State to provide proof of their allegations. The Commission reaffirms the general principle of law onus probandi actori incumbit according to which the burden of proof lies on the party who alleges. The corollary principle reus in exceptione fit actor allows the burden of proof to be shifted to the opposing party only when it has previously identified a failing on the part of the Complainant or when the latter has proved that he has discharged his initial obligation. This is not the case here and the burden of proof therefore remains on the Complainants. In view of these findings, the Commission concludes that local remedies existed but were not pursued.

In sum, the Commission finds that the Complainants have been unable to prove either the incompetence of the domestic courts or the non-existence of remedies to justify the application of a derogation from the exhaustion of local remedies on the basis of the serious and massive nature of the alleged violations. Furthermore, the Commission finds that the request for an exception based on the non-existence of local remedies owing to the fragility of the State's authority cannot succeed either. Without there being any need to examine the other arguments invoked by the Complainants, the Commission concludes that the Communication does not comply with the requirement laid down in Article 56(5) of the African Charter.

In view of the foregoing, the African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights: i. Declares this Communication inadmissible for non-compliance with the provisions of Article 56(5) of the African Charter; ii. Gives notice of the decision to the Parties and attaches it to its Activity Report in accordance with the provisions of Rule 107(3) of its Rules of Procedure. Adopted at the 18 Extraordinary Session of the African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights, held from 29 July to 7 August 2015, in Nairobi, Kenya.

Le 09 Mars 2010, le Secrétariat de la Commission africaine des droits de l'homme et des peuples (le Secrétariat) a reçu de Maître Feliho Kenneth (le Plaignant), une Communication introduite en vertu de l'article 55 de la Charte africaine des droits de l'homme et des peuples (la Charte africaine).

Cette Communication a été introduite au nom de Monsieur Kofi Yamgnane (la Victime) contre la République du Togo (le Togo ou l'Etat défendeur), Etat qui a ratifié la Charte africaine le 05 novembre 1982.

Le Plaignant indique que Monsieur Kofi Yamgnane a déposé sa candidature à l'élection présidentielle du 28 février 2010 et ce, en application des dispositions de l'article 83 du Code électoral togolais qui résulte de la rédaction modificative par la loi n° 2009-15 du 12 août 2009, ouvrant le droit à tout Togolais de faire acte de candidature.

Le Plaignant soutient que la Commission Electorale Nationale Indépendante (C.E.N.I) a soumis le dossier de candidature à la procédure d'examen et de vérification prévue par les dispositions de l'article 173 du Code électoral togolais.

Le Plaignant affirme qu'un récépissé définitif de candidature a été délivré par la C.E.N.I à Monsieur Kofi Yamgnane après dépôt du cautionnement au Trésor Public conformément aux dispositions de l'alinéa 2 de l'article 174 du Code électoral togolais.

Le Plaignant rapporte que le 25 janvier 2010, Monsieur Kofi Yamgnane a accusé réception d'un courrier émanant du Président de la Cour Constitutionnelle dans lequel sont reprises les observations du Ministre de l'Administration territoriale, de la Décentralisation et des Collectivités locales portant sur deux points ▪ Le premier concerne le contenu du dossier de candidature et conclut à un dépôt de pièces conformes aux dispositions du code électoral togolais ; ▪ Le second est relatif à l'authenticité des pièces et documents fournis par Monsieur Kofi Yamgnane et à ce propos, le Plaignant estime que le Ministre porte clairement un jugement de valeur sans équivoque puisqu'il considère : « ... Qu'il pèse sur le dossier de Monsieur Kofi Yamgnane, une multiplicité d'irrégularités qui se rapportent à son certificat de naissance, à son certificat de nationalité, à sa domiciliation effective pendant au moins douze mois au Togo et au nombre d'électeurs appuyant sa candidature. ».

Le Plaignant souligne que Monsieur Kofi Yamgnane qui a été sommé de répondre sous vingt-quatre heures au courrier du Président de la Cour Constitutionnelle l'a fait dans les délais en apportant toutes les clarifications nécessaires à la justification de la régularité et de la sincérité des pièces de son dossier. Malgré tout, la Cour Constitutionnelle a rendu le 02 février 2010, une décision qui rejette la candidature de Monsieur Kofi Yamgnane.

Le Plaignant soutient que l'auto-saisine de la Cour Constitutionnelle est illégale et que les effets de sa décision sont gravement attentatoires aux droits civils et politiques de la Victime. Il soutient en outre que la décision rendue par la Cour Constitutionnelle du Togo est insusceptible de recours.

Le Plaignant allègue également l'absence de séparation des pouvoirs et invoque à ce sujet, l'irrégularité de l'auto-saisine de la Cour Constitutionnelle togolaise qui a empiété sur les pouvoirs de la C.E.N.I qui, selon lui, était l'autorité compétente pour statuer sur les irrégularités éventuelles dans les dossiers de candidature à l'élection présidentielle.
Le Plaignant allègue la violation des articles 7 et 13 de la Charte africaine.

Le Plaignant demande à la Commission africaine des droits de l'homme et des peuples (la Commission) de : ▪ Recevoir et prendre acte de la Communication ; ▪ Constater que le candidat Kofi Yamgnane a été privé de ses droits politiques par une décision manifestement politique et de questionner l'autorité togolaise à ce propos ; ▪ Constater les manquements à la Charte africaine ratifiée par le Togo et de questionner l'autorité togolaise à ce propos ; ▪ Constater les violations du Code électoral par la Cour Constitutionnelle et questionner l'autorité togolaise à ce propos ; ▪ Constater qu'il est de fait privé de recours interne dans son pays puisque la décision contestable a été prise en premier et dernier ressort et que l'inexistence de juridictions administratives figent la situation du candidat et de questionner l'autorité togolaise à ce propos ; ▪ Considérer la demande gracieuse de soumission du problème à la Cour africaine des droits de l'homme et des peuples si l'Etat Togolais ne modifie pas sa position ; ▪ Œuvrer par tous les moyens nécessaires au respect de la Charte africaine par les Etats signataires.
La Communication a été déposée au Secrétariat le 09 mars 2010.
Lors de sa 47 Session ordinaire tenue du 12 au 26 mai 2010 à Banjul, en Gambie, la Commission s'est saisie de la Communication.
Par Note Verbale et lettre datées du 04 juin 2010, le Secrétariat a informé les Parties de la décision sur la saisine et les a invité à soumettre leurs observations sur la recevabilité.

Par Note Verbale et lettre datées du 25 octobre 2010, le Secrétariat a informé les Parties que la recevabilité de la Communication sera examinée par la Commission lors de sa 48 Session ordinaire. Le Secrétariat a à cet effet, invité l'Etat défendeur à soumettre ses observations sur la recevabilité.

Par Note Verbale en date du 14 juillet 2011, l'Etat défendeur informa le Secrétariat qu'il n'avait pas reçu copie de la Communication et l'a prié de lui faire parvenir une copie de la Communication ainsi que tout document pertinent y relatif.
Par lettre datée du 03 août 2011, le Plaignant a transmis ses observations complémentaires sur la recevabilité au Secrétariat qui en a accusé réception par lettre datée du 11 août 2011.

Par Notes Verbales du 03 août 2011 et du 11 août 2011, le Secrétariat a respectivement envoyé à l'Etat défendeur, une copie de la Communication et une copie des observations supplémentaires du Plaignant sur la recevabilité.
Par lettre datée du 20 septembre 2012, deux avocats ont transmis au Secrétariat, le mémoire de l'Etat défendeur sur la recevabilité de la Communication.

Par lettre datée du 30 septembre 2012, le Secrétariat a transmis au Plaignant, le mémoire de l'Etat défendeur sur la recevabilité et l'a invité à soumettre ses observations éventuelles sur ledit mémoire dans un délai d'un (01) mois conformément à l'article 105 (3) du Règlement intérieur de la Commission.

Par Note Verbale datée du 02 octobre 2012, l'Etat défendeur a invité la Commission à reporter l'examen de la Communication à sa 53 Session ordinaire afin de lui donner le temps de présenter son mémoire.

Par Note Verbale du 08 novembre 2012, le Secrétariat a indiqué à l'Etat défendeur qu'un mémoire sur la recevabilité de la Communication lui a été transmis par deux avocats indiquant agir pour l'Etat défendeur.

Le 27 décembre 2013, le Secrétariat a transmis une lettre datée du 23 décembre 2013 au Plaignant, l'informant que la Commission a examiné la Communication lors de sa 13 Session extraordinaire tenue du 19 au 25 février 2013 à Banjul, en Gambie, et l'a déclarée recevable. Le Secrétariat a par la même occasion, transmis la décision sur la recevabilité au Plaignant et l'a invité à soumettre ses observations sur le fond dans un délai de soixante (60) jours conformément à l'article 108 (1) du Règlement intérieur de la Commission.
Par Note Verbale datée du 23 décembre 2013, le Secrétariat a également informé l'Etat défendeur que la Commission est dans l'attente des observations du Plaignant sur le fond.

Le Plaignant n'ayant pas transmis ses observations sur le fond au terme du délai imparti, le Secrétariat a, par lettres datées du 26 mai 2014 et du 01 août 2014, informé le Plaignant que la Communication sera présentée à la Commission pour radiation.

Le Règlement intérieur de la Commission dispose en son article 108 (1) qu'une fois une Communication déclarée recevable, la Commission accorde un délai de soixante (60) jours au Plaignant pour transmettre ses observations sur le fond.

L'article 113 du Règlement intérieur dispose qu'une quelconque des Parties à une Communication peut demander à la Commission, la prorogation d'un délai qui lui est imparti pour la production d'un document ou la soumission d'arguments ou d'information. La Commission peut dans ce cas accorder une prorogation de délai qui n'excède pas un (01) mois.

Dans le cas d'espèce, le Plaignant a été invité depuis le 27 décembre 2013 à soumettre ses observations sur le fond de la Communication dans un délai soixante (60) jours. A l'expiration de ce délai et jusque-là, le Plaignant n'a pas transmis lesdites observations.

De surcroît, la Commission a perdu tout contact avec le Plaignant, n'ayant pas reçu de réponses de sa part à la suite des correspondances qui lui ont été envoyées depuis la transmission de la décision sur la recevabilité le 27 décembre 2013.

Au regard de ce qui précède, la Commission constate le manque de diligence du Plaignant quant à la poursuite de l'affaire et décide : i. de radier la Communication pour manque de diligence dans la poursuite de l'affaire ; et, ii. de notifier la décision aux Parties. Fait à Banjul, en Gambie, lors de la 17 Session extraordinaire de la Commission africaine des droits de l'homme et des peuples tenue du 19 au 28 février 2015

On 9 March 2010, the Secretariat of the African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights (the Secretariat) received from Maître Feliho Kenneth (the Complainant), a Communication submitted pursuant to Article 55 of the African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights (the African Charter).
This Communication was submitted on behalf of Mr Kofi Yamgnane (the Victim) against the Republic of Togo (Togo or the Respondent State), a State that ratified the African Charter on 5 November 1982.

The Complainant states that Mr Kofi Yamgnane submitted his candidacy for the presidential election of 28 February 2010, in application of the provisions of Article 83 of the Togolese Electoral Code as amended by Law No. 2009-15 of 12 August 2009, which gives every Togolese the right to stand as a candidate.

The Complainant submits that the Independent National Electoral Commission (C.E.N.I) subjected the candidacy file to the examination and verification procedure provided for by the provisions of Article 173 of the Togolese Electoral Code.

The Complainant asserts that a final receipt of candidacy was issued by the C.E.N.I to Mr Kofi Yamgnane after the deposit of the security with the Public Treasury in accordance with the provisions of paragraph 2 of Article 174 of the Togolese Electoral Code.

The Complainant reports that on 25 January 2010, Mr Kofi Yamgnane acknowledged receipt of a letter from the President of the Constitutional Court setting out the observations of the Minister of Territorial Administration, Decentralisation and Local Authorities on two points ▪ The first concerns the content of the candidacy file and concludes that the documents were filed in accordance with the provisions of the electoral code of Togo; ▪ The second relates to the authenticity of the documents and papers provided by Mr Kofi Yamgnane and in this regard, the Complainant is of the view that the Minister clearly makes an unequivocal value judgment since he considers: "... That Mr Kofi Yamgnane's file is affected by a multiplicity of irregularities relating to his birth certificate, his certificate of nationality, his effective residence for at least twelve months in Togo and the number of voters supporting his candidacy.".

The Complainant points out that Mr Kofi Yamgnane, who was summoned to reply within twenty-four hours to the letter from the President of the Constitutional Court, did so within the time limit, providing all the clarifications necessary to justify the regularity and sincerity of the documents in his file. Despite this, on 2 February 2010 the Constitutional Court delivered a decision rejecting Mr Kofi Yamgnane's candidacy.

The Complainant submits that the Constitutional Court's seizure of the matter of its own motion is illegal and that the effects of its decision seriously infringe the civil and political rights of the Victim. He further submits that the decision rendered by the Constitutional Court of Togo is not open to appeal.

The Complainant also alleges the absence of separation of powers and in this regard invokes the irregularity of the self-seizure of the Togolese Constitutional Court, which encroached upon the powers of the C.E.N.I, which, according to him, was the competent authority to rule on any irregularities in the candidacy files for the presidential election.
The Complainant alleges the violation of Articles 7 and 13 of the African Charter.

The Complainant requests the African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights (the Commission) to: ▪ Receive and take note of the Communication; ▪ Find that the candidate Kofi Yamgnane was deprived of his political rights by a manifestly political decision and question the Togolese authorities in this regard; ▪ Find the breaches of the African Charter ratified by Togo and question the Togolese authorities in this regard; ▪ Find the violations of the Electoral Code by the Constitutional Court and question the Togolese authorities in this regard; ▪ Find that he is in fact deprived of domestic remedies in his country since the contested decision was taken at first and last instance and that the non-existence of administrative courts freezes the situation of the candidate, and question the Togolese authorities in this regard; ▪ Consider the gracious request to submit the problem to the African Court on Human and Peoples' Rights if the Togolese State does not change its position; ▪ Work by all necessary means towards respect for the African Charter by the signatory States.
The Communication was received at the Secretariat on 9 March 2010.
At its 47th Ordinary Session held from 12 to 26 May 2010 in Banjul, The Gambia, the Commission was seized of the Communication.
By Note Verbale and letter dated 4 June 2010, the Secretariat informed the Parties of the decision on seizure and invited them to submit their observations on admissibility.

By Note Verbale and letter dated 25 October 2010, the Secretariat informed the Parties that the admissibility of the Communication would be considered by the Commission at its 48th Ordinary Session. To that end, the Secretariat invited the Respondent State to submit its observations on admissibility.

By Note Verbale dated 14 July 2011, the Respondent State informed the Secretariat that it had not received a copy of the Communication and requested it to send it a copy of the Communication together with any relevant documents relating thereto.
By letter dated 3 August 2011, the Complainant transmitted his additional observations on admissibility to the Secretariat, which acknowledged receipt by letter dated 11 August 2011.

By Notes Verbales of 3 August 2011 and 11 August 2011, the Secretariat sent to the Respondent State, respectively, a copy of the Communication and a copy of the Complainant's additional observations on admissibility.
By letter dated 20 September 2012, two lawyers transmitted to the Secretariat the Respondent State's brief on the admissibility of the Communication.

By letter dated 30 September 2012, the Secretariat transmitted to the Complainant the Respondent State's brief on admissibility and invited him to submit his possible observations on the said brief within one (01) month in accordance with Rule 105(3) of the Commission's Rules of Procedure.

By Note Verbale dated 2 October 2012, the Respondent State invited the Commission to postpone consideration of the Communication to its 53rd Ordinary Session in order to give it time to present its brief.

By Note Verbale of 8 November 2012, the Secretariat indicated to the Respondent State that a brief on the admissibility of the Communication had been transmitted to it by two lawyers stating that they were acting for the Respondent State.

On 27 December 2013, the Secretariat transmitted a letter dated 23 December 2013 to the Complainant, informing him that the Commission had considered the Communication during its 13th Extraordinary Session held from 19 to 25 February 2013 in Banjul, The Gambia, and had declared it admissible. The Secretariat at the same time transmitted the decision on admissibility to the Complainant and invited him to submit his observations on the merits within sixty (60) days in accordance with Rule 108(1) of the Commission's Rules of Procedure.
By Note Verbale dated 23 December 2013, the Secretariat also informed the Respondent State that the Commission was awaiting the Complainant's observations on the merits.

As the Complainant had not transmitted his observations on the merits at the end of the allotted time, the Secretariat, by letters dated 26 May 2014 and 1 August 2014, informed the Complainant that the Communication would be presented to the Commission for striking out.

The Commission's Rules of Procedure provide in Rule 108(1) that once a Communication has been declared admissible, the Commission grants the Complainant a period of sixty (60) days to transmit his observations on the merits.

Rule 113 of the Rules of Procedure provides that any of the Parties to a Communication may request the Commission for an extension of a time limit allotted to it for the production of a document or the submission of arguments or information. In that case, the Commission may grant an extension of time which does not exceed one (01) month.

In the present case, the Complainant was invited as of 27 December 2013 to submit his observations on the merits of the Communication within sixty (60) days. Upon expiry of that period and until now, the Complainant has not transmitted the said observations.

Moreover, the Commission has lost all contact with the Complainant, having received no replies from him to the correspondence sent to him since the transmission of the decision on admissibility on 27 December 2013.

In light of the foregoing, the Commission notes the Complainant's lack of diligence in pursuing the case and decides: i. to strike out the Communication for lack of diligence in pursuing the case; and, ii. to notify the decision to the Parties. Done in Banjul, The Gambia, during the 17th Extraordinary Session of the African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights held from 19 to 28 February 2015

The Secretariat of the African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights (the Secretariat) received a Complaint on 25 October 2012 from the Socio-Economic Rights and Accountability Project - SERAP (the Complainant), against the Federal Republic of Nigeria (the Respondent State). SERAP is a Nigerian registered human rights organization with Observer Status with the Commission. The Complaint is submitted in terms of Article 55 and 56 of the African Charter on Human and Peoples Rights, (the African Charter).
The Respondent State is a State Party to the African Charter having ratified the same on 1 October 1984.

The Complainant alleges that despite its obligations under the African Charter and other international treaties to which it is a Party, the Government of the Respondent State, through the Edo State authorities, has violated the right to a fair trial of Daniel Nsofor and Osayinwinde Agbomien (the Victims), who are two death row inmates at the Edo State Prison. It alleges that the Respondent State has committed serious, persistent and irreparable violations of the Victims' rights: to life; to competent and effective legal representation; to trial by a competent, independent and impartial tribunal established by law; to the presumption of innocence; to appeal to an independent and impartial tribunal; and to fair trial guarantees during appeals.

The Complainant further alleges that the Victims are at risk of imminent execution, having been convicted of murder. Under Nigeria's penal laws the death penalty is mandatory for murder. The Complainant states that in March 2010, a Nigerian NGO - Legal Defence and Advocacy Project (LEDAP) - had filed an Appeal on behalf of 840 inmates - including the Victims, following which an injunction was granted by the court upholding the Appeal, but which was later lifted in April 2012. The Complainant states that LEDAP subsequently filed another Appeal in April 2012 following the court's decision, and that the judgment on that Appeal is pending.

The Complainant alleges that it has received reports that the gallows at the Benin prison, in Edo State, were inspected and tested on 22 October 2012, and that it feared that the Victims would be executed by the Edo State Authorities. The Complainant avers that the decision by the Governor of Edo State to sign the death warrants of the Victims, whilst their Appeal is pending, constitutes a fundamental breach of their right to fair trial, including the right to an appeal to an independent and impartial tribunal.

The Complainant further alleges that the Governor of Edo State signed the execution warrants two weeks after prison authorities informed him that death row inmates in the Benin prison were 'becoming unmanageable.' It informs the Commission that some death row inmates had been involved in a recent jailbreak incident in Oko prison in Edo State. The Complainant alleges that as a means to decongest the country prisons, the resumption of executions by Edo State follows an announcement by State Governors in June 2011 that they would review all cases of death row inmates and sign off executions as a means of decongesting the country's prisons.

The Complainant argues that the planned execution of the Victims on the sole ground that they are 'becoming unmanageable' while they still have their appeal pending, does not offer a fair and effective solution to the perceived problem of prison overcrowding.

The Complainant alleges that not only have the Victims been deprived of their liberty and other fair trial rights, but also alleges that the Victims' conditions are now characterized by depression, loss of sense of reality and physical and mental deterioration; massive deprivation of personal autonomy critical to psychological survival; and emotional emptiness.

The Complainant avers that the 2004 National Study Group on Death Penalty and the 2007 Presidential Commission on the Administration of Justice both stressed that the Nigerian criminal justice system cannot guarantee a fair trial, and called for a moratorium on the death penalty.

Quoting the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, the Complainant states that "recognition of the inherent dignity and the equal and inalienable rights of all members of the human family is the foundation of freedom, justice and peace in the world", that "[e]veryone is entitled in full equality to a fair and public hearing... of any criminal charge", and that "[e]veryone charged with a penal offence has the right to be presumed innocent until proven guilty according to law in a public trial".

It further argues that the right to a fair trial is a fundamental safeguard to ensure that individuals are not unjustly punished. It is indispensable for the protection of other human rights such as the right to freedom from torture and cruel or inhuman treatment, and the right to life. It states that, however, when people are subjected to unfair trials, justice cannot be served.

The Complainant further states that the Commission at its 44 Ordinary Session in Abuja, Nigeria, in November 2008 adopted a resolution calling on African States, including Nigeria, that still retain the death penalty to "observe a moratorium on the execution of death sentences with a view to abolishing the death penalty." It avers that the resolution recalled Article 4 of the African Charter, which recognizes the right of everyone to life, and Article 5(3) of the African Charter on the Rights and the Welfare of the Child, which guarantees the non-application of death penalty for crimes committed by children. The resolution expresses concerns about "the failure of some African states [including Nigeria] to give effect to the UN resolutions and African Commission's own 1999 resolution calling for a moratorium on executions", and about the application of "the death penalty in conditions not respectful of the right to a fair trial guaranteed under the African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights and other relevant international norms".

The Complainant states that the resolution also asked AU member states, including Nigeria, that still retain the death penalty to: fully comply with their obligations under the African Charter and guarantee to every person accused of crimes for which capital punishment is applicable, fair trial standards; and to include in their periodic reports information on the steps they are taking to move towards the abolition of the death penalty in their countries.

The Complainant states that it considers that the application of the death penalty in these cases will be illegal and unjust. The Complainant further considers supervening factors such as those highlighted above to be sufficient grounds for stopping the Edo State authorities from going ahead with the planned execution of prisoners on death row with the unjustified and illegitimate ground that the prisoners are "becoming unmanageable". The Complainant argues that prisoners are not denuded of their rights by mere conviction. If carried out, the death sentences on the Victims would amount to inhuman or degrading treatment and unfair trial as many of the prisoners on death row have not exhausted their right to appeal.

The Complainant concedes that generally, local remedies must be exhausted prior to submitting a Communication to the Commission. However, it submits that there are exceptions to this general rule, as the Commission has stated that local remedies must be available, effective and sufficient. It avers that a local remedy is considered available if the petitioner can pursue it without impediment; it is effective if it offers a prospect of success and it is sufficient if it is capable of redressing the complaint. It claims that the Victims' case before the Nigerian court of appeal has been ignored by Respondent State.
The Complainant alleges that the Respondent State has violated Articles 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, and 7 of African Charter.

The Complainant prays the African Commission to: (i) Consider the present Communication under Articles 55, 56 and 58 of the African Charter, and to undertake an in-depth study, based on the "series of serious" and "massive" violations alleged in this Communication; (ii) Find the Respondent State to be in violation of the Victims' right to life under Article 4 of the African Charter; and (iii) Request the Respondent State to pay appropriate compensation to the Victims for the multiple violations of their Charter rights and freedoms.

The Communication was received at the Secretariat on 25 October 2012. During its 13 Extra-Ordinary Session held from 19 – 25 February 2013, the Commission considered the Communication and was seized of it. On 4 March 2013 and 5 March 2013, Complainant and the Respondent State were respectively informed of the Seizure decision, and the Complainant was requested to forward its submission on the Admissibility of the Communication within two months of notification, in accordance with Rule 105(1) of the Commission's Rules of Procedure; that is, by 3 May 2013.

The Communication was considered between the 14 Extra-Ordinary Session of the Commission held from 20 - 24 July 2013 and its 18 Extra-Ordinary Session held from 29 July – 7 August 2015, but deferred due to non-submission of the Complainant's arguments on Admissibility.

Rule 105(1) of the Commission's Rules of Procedure establishes that when the Commission has decided to be seized of a Communication, it shall request the Complainant to present arguments on Admissibility within two (2) months.

Rule 113 of the Commission's Rules of Procedure provides that when a deadline is fixed for a particular submission, either party may apply to the Commission for extension of the period stipulated. The Commission may grant an extension of time for a period not longer than one (1) month.
To date, and more than two (2) years after the stipulated deadline, the Complainant has not (i) made any admissibility submissions, and (ii) has not requested for an extension of time to submit.
Consequently the Commission does not have sufficient information upon which to make a determination on the admissibility of the Communication.

In view of the above, the Commission decides to strike out the Communication for lack of diligent prosecution. Done in Banjul, The Gambia, during the 57 Ordinary Session of the African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights, 4 to 18 November, 2015

THOMPSON, Vice President, Justices Sophia A. B. AKUFFO, Bernard M. NGOEPE and Duncan TAMBALA 1. While we agree substantially with the outcome of the majority judgment, there is FIRSTLY, one particular point on which we disagree. Although this point is not material to the outcome of the case, it is in our view nevertheless important, inasmuch as the majority view on it purports to be an accurate reflection of the content of Rule 39(1) of the Rules of Court. We clarify from the outset that there is nothing wrong in starting

with the examination of jurisdiction first, and then deal with admissibility later, as the majority judgment does. It, however, needs to be mentioned that there has never been unanimity in this Court that that should necessarily always be the case; there has always been a view that it would not necessarily be wrong, in a given case, to examine admissibility first. 2. The above debate cannot be resolved in favour of starting with jurisdiction, by, as the majority judgment seeks to do, importing into Rule 39(1) a word which is not in there, namely, the word "first". Apparently, the importation is made to strengthen the case for starting with jurisdiction first as opposed to admissibility. The relevant paragraph of the majority judgment, being paragraph 30, reads: " Rule 39(1) of the Rules ... provides that the Court must first conduct preliminary examination of its jurisdiction " (own underlining). Yet, with respect, the Rule does not say that; it reads: " The Court shall conduct preliminary examination of its jurisdiction and the admissibility of the application ... ". The word "first" appears nowhere in the Rule, let alone specifically prescribing that one should start with jurisdiction first. Whatever reason may be behind importing that word into the Rule, it remains factually incorrect to say, as the majority judgment does, that the Rule contains that particular word, when it does not; accordingly, we disagree with that statement. It may well be that starting with jurisdiction may be justified on

other premises. We say nothing more, as we do not wish to enter the debate referred to in paragraph 1 above. 3. SECONDLY, regarding the merits, we would, while agreeing with the outcome of the majority judgment, have in some respects approached the matter differently and also framed the Orders differently. 4. Having found that the application is admissible and that the Court has jurisdiction, we would zoom onto the crisp question in the matter: are the Burkinabe laws in terms of which the Applicant was convicted of defamation, namely, Articles 109 and 110 of the Information Code, and Article 178 of the Penal Code, in conflict with Article 9 of the African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights, and other instruments relied upon and cited by the Applicant? In our view, the answer is in the affirmative. As presently framed, the above legislative measure are, for the reasons set out in the majority judgment, an unjustified restriction to the right of freedom of expression; that is, criminalization of defamation is not justified. If such criminalization can be justified under certain circumstances, such as prohibiting for example hate speech or incitement, the above legislative measures, as they currently read, are too broad and problematic. It must be mentioned though, that the possible exceptions referred to are more theoretical than real. This is because once a so-called criminal defamation amounts to say hate speech or incitement, it is no longer criminal defamation; it mutates into one of the already existing and well known specific crimes such as Two handwritten signatures are visible at the bottom right of the page. The signature on the left is a simple, stylized 'R' or 'L' shape. The signature on the right is more complex, featuring a large, bold 'S' or 'P' followed by several horizontal strokes.

sedition or high treason and there would be no talk of criminal defamation. The State's duty to enforce the obligation on an individual under Article 27(2) of the Charter to exercise rights " with due regard to the rights of others, collective security, morality and common interest " cannot justify the criminalization of expression of speech by way of criminal defamation laws of any kind, whether punishable by incarceration or not. Access to civil action, civil sanction, together with specifically defined crimes for safeguarding national security, public peace and the common interest, should be sufficient. For this Court to hold otherwise would not only be a step backward in the evolution of human rights in Africa, but also out of consonance with the letter and spirit of the Charter, which it is established to uphold. 5. Finally, given our view that the Applicant's conviction was in the first place invalid, it is immaterial whether the punishments imposed are excessive or lenient. There should have been no punishment based on criminal defamation at all; the aggrieved person should have resorted to other avenues than to criminal recourse. Subject of the Application 1. The Court is seized of this matter by way of an Application dated 14 June 2013 and filed by Barristers John R.W.D Jones, Q.C and Yakaré-Oulé (Nani) Jansen, acting on behalf of Lohé Issa Konaté, a Burkinabé national and Editor-in-Chief of L'Ouragan Weekly published in Burkina Faso; the Application was received at the Registry on 17 June 2013 and registered as No. 004/2013.
Attached to the Application is a request for provisional measures on which the Court ruled by Order dated 4 October 2013.

Prosecution for defamation, public insult and contempt of Court was initiated against the Applicant following the publication, in L'Ouragan on 1 August 2012, of an article written by him and titled "Contrefaçon et trafic de faux billets de banque – Le Procureur du Faso, 3 policiers et un cadre de banque, parrains des bandits" ("Counterfeiting and laundering of fake bank notes – the Prosecutor of Faso, 3 Police Officers and a Bank Official – Masterminds of Banditry") as well as an Article by Roland Ouédraogo titled "Le Procureur du Faso: un torpilleur de la justice". (The Prosecutor of Faso – a saboteur of Justice"). The Applicant had published a second article written by himself in another issue of L'Ouragan dated 8 August 2012; that article was titled "Déni de justice – Procureur du Faso: un justicier voyou?". ("Miscarriage of Justice – the Prosecutor of Faso: a rogue officer").

Having been accused in all three above-mentioned articles, the Prosecutor, Placide Nikiéma, filed a complaint for defamation, public insult and contempt of Court, against the Applicant and Mr. Ouédraogo. It is on these grounds that criminal proceedings were brought and damages sought, against the Applicant, before the Ouagadougou High Court.

On 29 October 2012, the Ouagadougou High Court sentenced the Applicant to a twelve (12) month term of imprisonment and ordered him to pay a fine of 1.5 Million CFA Francs (an equivalent of 3000USD), the same court ordered the Applicant to pay the Complainant damages of 4.5 Million CFA Francs (an equivalent of 9000USD) as damages and interest, and court costs of 250,000 CFA Francs (an equivalent of 500USD).

Further, as additional penalties, the Court ordered that L'Ouragan Weekly be suspended for a period of six (6) months and for the operative provisions of the judgment to be published in three successive issues of L'Evenement, L'Observateur Paalga, Le Pays and L'Ouragan Newspapers and, in the case of the latter, in its first issue upon its resumption of activity and for a period of four months, at the cost of the Applicant and Mr. Roland Ouedraogo.
On 10 May 2013, the Ouagadougou Court of Appeal confirmed the judgment of the Ouagadougou High Court.

The Applicant alleges that L'Ouragan is a private Weekly with "an independent editorial policy focussing mainly on political and social issues"; that the paper "has been the object of various legal proceedings in Burkina Faso due to its style in news reporting".

The Applicant submits in his Application that "the jail term, huge fine, damages as well as the court costs violate his right to freedom of expression which is protected under various treaties to which Burkina Faso is a Party"; he also alleges notably the violation of his rights under Article 9 of the African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights (hereinafter referred to as "the Charter"), and Article 19 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (hereinafter, referred to as "the Covenant").

10. Article 9 of the Charter provides as follows: “1) Every individual shall have the right to receive information. 2) Every individual shall have the right to express and disseminate his opinions within the laws and regulations”.

Article 19 of the Covenant, for its part, provides that: “1. Everyone shall have the right to hold opinions without interference. 2. Everyone shall have the right to freedom of expression; this right shall include freedom to seek, receive and impart information and ideas of all kinds, regardless of frontiers, either orally, in writing or in print, in the form of art, or through any other media of his choice. 3. The exercise of the rights provided for in paragraph 2 of this article carries with it special duties and responsibilities. It may therefore be subject to certain restrictions, but these shall only be such as are provided by law and are necessary: (a) For respect of the rights or reputations of others; (b) For the protection of national security or of public order or of public health or morals”.
